Q59095: Coastal city in Guangdong on the Pearl River estuary, bordering Macau; the name means 'pearl sea'.
One of China's first four Special Economic Zones (1980).
The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge (55 km, opened 2018) is the world's longest sea crossing.
Known as a clean, green resort city and for the Zhuhai Airshow.
Q43433: Planned city and union territory, the shared capital of Punjab and Haryana states.
Designed by Le Corbusier in the 1950s after Lahore went to Pakistan; his Capitol Complex is a World Heritage Site.
Laid out in numbered sectors at the foot of the Shivalik hills.
Known for Nek Chand's Rock Garden, made from recycled waste.
Q40236: Capital of Amazonas, in the middle of the Amazon rainforest near where the Rio Negro meets the Amazon.
Grew rich in the rubber boom around 1900, when it built the famous Teatro Amazonas opera house.
The 'Meeting of the Waters': the dark Rio Negro and the sandy Solimões flow side by side without mixing for kilometres.
A free-trade zone with factories for electronics and motorcycles.
Q41211: Capital of Puerto Rico, a US territory in the Caribbean.
Founded by the Spanish in 1521: the oldest city under US sovereignty.
Old San Juan, with the El Morro and San Cristóbal fortresses, is a World Heritage Site.
La Fortaleza is the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas.
Q171632: Venezuela's second-largest city, on the strait linking Lake Maracaibo with the Caribbean.
Centre of the Venezuelan oil industry since oil was found around the lake in 1914.
The General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge (8.7 km) crosses the lake's outlet.
Famous for gaita music; one of the hottest cities in South America.
Q5806: The holiest city in Islam, in western Saudi Arabia; birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad.
The Great Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) surrounds the Kaaba, the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide.
Millions of Muslims make the Hajj pilgrimage here each year; non-Muslims are not allowed to enter.
Overlooked by the Abraj Al-Bait clock towers, among the tallest buildings in the world.
Q6487: City on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, the centre of the Turkish Riviera and the country's tourism capital.
Founded around 200 BC by King Attalus II of Pergamon as Attaleia.
Hadrian's Gate and the Kaleiçi old town survive; ancient Perge, Aspendos and Side are nearby.
Q1850: Capital of Cambodia, where the Tonlé Sap and Mekong rivers meet.
Named after Wat Phnom temple and Lady Penh, the legendary founder.
Emptied by the Khmer Rouge in 1975; the Tuol Sleng (S-21) prison is now a genocide museum.
The Royal Palace and Silver Pagoda are landmarks; once called the 'Pearl of Asia'.
Q569907: Industrial city in Inner Mongolia on the Yellow River; the name means 'place with deer' in Mongolian.
Called the 'City of Steel on the Grasslands' for its big steelworks.
Mines and refines over half of the world's rare-earth metals (from Bayan Obo).
Its rare-earth waste lake is notorious for pollution.
Q3820: Capital of Lebanon, on a peninsula on the Mediterranean; inhabited for over 5,000 years.
Once called the 'Paris of the Middle East' for its cosmopolitan culture and banking.
Heavily damaged in the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990).
A huge explosion of stored ammonium nitrate in its port in 2020 killed over 200 people.
Q3792: Capital of Togo, on the Gulf of Guinea right at the border with Ghana.
The city centre is only a few hundred metres from the Ghanaian border.
Its deep-water port is one of the busiest in West Africa.
Known for the Akodessewa fetish market of voodoo items.
Q2568315: Coastal town in Kerala at the mouth of the Bharathappuzha, Kerala's second-longest river.
Called the 'little Mecca of Kerala' for its role in Islamic learning; the Ponnani Juma Masjid dates from the 16th century.
An old port of the Zamorin kings.
Q57906: City in Jiangsu on the Grand Canal near the Yangtze; one of the richest cities of imperial China thanks to the salt trade.
Marco Polo claimed to have governed it; the monk Jianzhen (Ganjin) sailed from here to Japan.
Famous for its gardens and Slender West Lake.
Origin of Yangzhou fried rice and a style of cuisine (Huaiyang).
Q62823: Colombia's main Caribbean port, near the mouth of the Magdalena River.
Its Carnival is one of the biggest in the world and a UNESCO intangible heritage.
An entry point for immigrants and home of SCADTA (1919), one of the first airlines in the Americas; called the 'Golden Gate of Colombia'.
Q5092: The largest city in Maryland, on Chesapeake Bay; nicknamed 'Charm City'.
During the War of 1812, the defence of Fort McHenry inspired the US national anthem, 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.
Home of Johns Hopkins University and hospital.
Known for its Inner Harbor and blue crabs.
Q207098: City in Uttar Pradesh, part of the Delhi National Capital Region on Delhi's eastern edge.
Called the 'Gateway of Uttar Pradesh' on the main route from Delhi.
A major industrial area and railway junction.
Founded in 1740 by vizier Ghazi-ud-din, after whom it is named.
Q35493: Kazakhstan's largest city, at the foot of the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains in the southeast.
Capital until 1997, when the government moved to Astana; still the economic centre.
The name means 'place of apples' — the wild ancestor of the domestic apple comes from this region.
Medeu, a high-altitude skating rink, and Shymbulak ski resort are just above the city.
Q16565: The largest city in North Carolina; named after Queen Charlotte, wife of King George III.
The second-largest banking centre in the US, headquarters of Bank of America.
Home of the NASCAR Hall of Fame; much of NASCAR is based nearby.
Q28994: City in northern Guizhou between Guiyang and Chongqing.
The 1935 Zunyi Conference during the Long March made Mao Zedong a leader of the Communist Party.
Maotai, home of China's most famous liquor (baijiu), is in the prefecture.
Known for its red-tourism sites and tea.
Q115256: Special municipality in northwestern Taiwan, southwest of Taipei.
Home of Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, the country's main airport.
Has many industrial parks and the fastest population growth in Taiwan.
Q11506: Capital of Bali, the largest city in the Lesser Sunda Islands.
Gateway for Bali's tourism; Kuta and Sanur beaches lie at its edge.
Site of the 1906 puputan, a mass ritual suicide of the Badung royal court facing Dutch troops.
Q200235: City on the Godavari River in Maharashtra.
One of four sites of the Kumbh Mela, the huge Hindu pilgrimage held every 12 years.
In the Ramayana, Lakshmana cut off the nose (nasika) of Surpanakha here — a legend for the city's name.
Called the 'Wine Capital of India' for its vineyards (Sula Vineyards).
Q200017: Commercial city in Andhra Pradesh on the Krishna River.
The Prakasam Barrage across the Krishna irrigates a large delta.
Home of the Kanaka Durga Temple on Indrakeeladri hill.
Part of the capital region around Amaravati, the planned new state capital.
Q162442: City in Uttar Pradesh, formerly Allahabad, at the confluence (Sangam) of the Ganges, Yamuna and mythical Sarasvati.
Hosts the Kumbh Mela, the largest religious gathering in the world (2025: hundreds of millions of visitors).
Birthplace of Jawaharlal Nehru; centre of the Indian independence movement.
Seat of the Allahabad High Court, one of the oldest in India.
Q46747: Capital of Miyagi Prefecture, the largest city in the Tōhoku region of northern Honshu.
Founded in 1600 by the one-eyed samurai lord Date Masamune.
Nicknamed the 'City of Trees'; hosts Japan's largest Tanabata festival.
Severely affected by the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami.
Q160320: Capital of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, on the Persian Gulf.
Oil was first found in Saudi Arabia here in 1938 (Dammam No. 7 'Prosperity Well').
Forms a metro area with Khobar and Dhahran, home of Saudi Aramco.
Connected to Bahrain by the King Fahd Causeway.
Q124739: The largest city of Baja California, on the US border next to San Diego.
Its San Ysidro crossing is one of the busiest land border crossings in the world.
Grew as a getaway for Americans during Prohibition; claims the invention of the Caesar salad.
A big centre of maquiladora factories (e.g. TVs and medical devices).
Q42053: Iran's third city, in the centre of the country on the Zayanderud River.
Capital of Safavid Persia under Shah Abbas I from 1598; people said 'Isfahan is half the world'.
Its Naqsh-e Jahan Square, one of the largest city squares in the world, is a World Heritage Site.
Known for its old covered bridges (Si-o-se-pol), tiled mosques and Persian carpets.
Q71284: City in northwestern Hubei on the Han River, formed from Xiangyang and Fancheng.
Famous in the Three Kingdoms story; Zhuge Liang lived nearby.
The Siege of Xiangyang (1267–1273) by the Mongols was a turning point in the conquest of Song China.
Has one of the oldest intact city walls and widest moats in China.
Q68579: City in Fujian on the Taiwan Strait.
Birthplace of Mazu, the sea goddess worshipped across southern China and Taiwan; her temple is on Meizhou Island.
Known for longans and lychees, and for its many shoe factories.
Q16559: Capital of Texas, on the Colorado River in the Texas Hill Country.
Calls itself the 'Live Music Capital of the World'; hosts the SXSW festival.
Home of the University of Texas and a booming tech scene ('Silicon Hills') with Tesla's Gigafactory.
Its Congress Avenue Bridge hosts the largest urban bat colony in North America.
Q147187: Site of the 1938 Battle of Taierzhuang, the first major Chinese victory over Japan in WWII.
Its Taierzhuang ancient town on the Grand Canal has been rebuilt.
Q57866: City on the Yellow Sea coast of Jiangsu; the name means 'Salt City'.
Sea salt has been produced here since the Han dynasty.
Its coastal wetlands are a World Heritage Site and a winter home of the red-crowned crane, with an elk (Père David's deer) reserve.
Home of a Kia car plant.
Q18013: Capital of California, where the Sacramento and American rivers meet.
Grew rapidly in the 1849 Gold Rush; gold was found at nearby Sutter's Mill.
Western end of the first transcontinental railroad (1869) and the Pony Express.
Q6106: The largest city in Oregon, where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet.
Its name was decided by a coin toss in 1845 (the other option was Boston).
Known for its bridges, food carts, Powell's bookshop and views of Mount Hood.
Headquarters of Nike is nearby in Beaverton.
Q359990: City in Anhui on the Yangtze River, southwest of Nanjing.
Historically one of China's four great rice markets.
Home of the carmaker Chery and the Fantawild theme parks.
Known for iron pictures (tiehua), a local art.
Q38022: City in Missouri near where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet.
Founded by French fur traders in 1764 and named after King Louis IX.
The 192 m Gateway Arch marks its role as the 'Gateway to the West' for the Lewis and Clark expedition and pioneers.
Hosted the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics; home of the blues and Budweiser beer.
Q14634: Capital of South Sulawesi, the largest city of eastern Indonesia; called Ujung Pandang from 1971 to 1999.
Centre of the Gowa Sultanate, which the Dutch conquered in the 17th century; Fort Rotterdam survives.
Makassarese sailors fished for sea cucumbers as far as northern Australia.
Known for its Losari Beach sunsets and phinisi wooden sailing ships.
Q200123: The largest city in Indian Punjab, near the Sutlej River.
Called the 'Manchester of India' for its hosiery and woollen knitwear.
India's biggest bicycle manufacturing centre (Hero Cycles).
Known for the Punjab Agricultural University, important for the Green Revolution.
Q426130: Second-largest city of Sichuan, northeast of Chengdu.
China's 'Science City': home of the China Academy of Engineering Physics, which developed nuclear weapons.
Birthplace of the Tang poet Li Bai (in Jiangyou).
Badly hit by the 2008 Sichuan earthquake.
Q79857: City on the Central Anatolian Plateau in Turkey; called Iconium in antiquity.
Capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in the Middle Ages.
The poet Rumi lived and is buried here; it is the home of the Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes'.
Çatalhöyük, one of the oldest towns in the world (about 9,000 years old), is nearby.
Q26600: The largest city on Kyushu, on Hakata Bay; Japan's closest big city to the Asian mainland.
Kublai Khan's Mongol invasion fleets were destroyed here in 1274 and 1281 (the 'kamikaze' divine winds).
Famous for Hakata tonkotsu ramen and street food stalls (yatai).
Formed from the merger of the castle town Fukuoka and the merchant town Hakata.
Q1163503: Metropolitan area of Espírito Santo, Brazil, around the island capital Vitória.
Includes Vila Velha, Serra and Cariacica; Vila Velha is the state's oldest town (1535).
A major port for exporting iron ore and steel.
The Convento da Penha on a hill is the main landmark.
Q200237: City in Uttar Pradesh, part of the Delhi National Capital Region.
The Indian Rebellion of 1857 started here when sepoys mutinied on 10 May.
One of the biggest army cantonments in India.
Known as India's sports goods capital (cricket bats and balls).
Q14773: A special administrative region of China across the Pearl River estuary from Hong Kong; the most densely populated region in the world.
A Portuguese trading post from 1557 and colony until 1999 — the last European colony in Asia.
The world's biggest gambling centre, earning more from casinos than Las Vegas.
Its historic centre, with the ruins of St. Paul's, is a World Heritage Site; known for Portuguese egg tarts.
Q58273: Coastal city in Zhejiang, between Ningbo and Wenzhou.
Known for private enterprise: a pioneer of shareholding cooperative companies in the 1980s.
Home of the Geely car company's first factories.
The Tiantai Mountain, birthplace of Tiantai Buddhism, is in the prefecture.
Q3861: Capital of Qatar, on the Persian Gulf; home to most of the country's people.
Grew from a pearling and fishing village into a modern city with natural-gas wealth.
Home of Al Jazeera and the Museum of Islamic Art.
Q181557: Taiwan's third city and main port, in the south of the island.
Centre of heavy industry: steel, oil refining and shipbuilding.
Called Takao under Japanese rule; known for Love River and the Lotus Pond pagodas.
Q706161: County-level city in Zhejiang under Ningbo, on Hangzhou Bay.
A big centre of household appliance manufacturing.
The Hangzhou Bay Bridge connects it to the Shanghai area.
Q3070: Capital of Costa Rica, in the Central Valley.
Was one of the first cities in the world with public electric street lighting (1884).
Known for the National Theatre and the pre-Columbian Gold Museum.
Q3183: Capital of Western Australia, on the Swan River near the Indian Ocean.
Often called the most isolated big city in the world (Adelaide is over 2,000 km away).
Founded in 1829 as the Swan River Colony; boomed with gold and later iron-ore mining.
Known for Kings Park and quokkas on nearby Rottnest Island.
Q427265: City in Sichuan where the Min and Jinsha rivers meet — often called the start of the Yangtze proper.
Famous for Wuliangye, one of China's top baijiu liquors.
A battery-making centre with a large CATL plant.
Known for burning noodles (ranmian) and the Shunan Bamboo Sea.
Q11854: City in Gujarat, centre of the Saurashtra peninsula.
Mahatma Gandhi grew up here; his father was the prime minister (diwan) of Rajkot State.
Capital of the short-lived Saurashtra State (1948–56).
Known for engineering industries and jewellery.
Q3921: Capital of Zimbabwe, on a highland plateau at about 1,500 m.
Founded in 1890 as Fort Salisbury by the British South Africa Company; renamed Harare in 1982.
Was the capital of Southern Rhodesia and the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
Known for its jacaranda-lined streets and Mbare market.
Q240: Capital of Belgium and the de facto capital of the European Union (European Commission, Council, Parliament).
Its Grand-Place, with ornate guild houses, is a World Heritage Site; the Atomium was built for Expo 58.
Officially bilingual (French and Dutch); known for waffles, chocolate, comics and the Manneken Pis.
Q228405: City on the Vaigai River in Tamil Nadu; one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in India.
Capital of the Pandya kings; the Tamil Sangam literature gatherings were held here.
The Meenakshi Amman Temple with its huge colourful towers (gopurams) is the city's heart.
Q8131: Capital of South Sumatra, on both banks of the Musi River.
Centre of the Srivijaya empire, a Buddhist maritime power in the 7th–13th centuries.
The Ampera Bridge is its symbol.
Famous for pempek fish cakes and co-hosted the 2018 Asian Games.
Q49233: City in Central Florida, the theme-park capital of the world.
Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando and SeaWorld are in the area.
One of the most visited cities in the US.
Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral is about an hour east.
Q59132: City in Guangdong on the western Pearl River Delta.
Ancestral home of about 4 million overseas Chinese, especially in North America.
Its Kaiping diaolou, fortified tower houses built with emigrants' money, are a World Heritage Site.
Known as 'China's first home of overseas Chinese'.
Q72818: Vietnam's main northern port, on the Gulf of Tonkin; the third-largest city.
Nicknamed the 'City of Red Flamboyant Flowers'.
Includes Cát Bà Island, next to Hạ Long Bay.
Heavily bombed in the Vietnam War; home of VinFast car factory.
